title: رافينيا بعد ثنائيته في أستون فيلا: لن أتحدث عن كرة القدم

body: Editor's note: The latest estimates from the Aerospace Corporation predict Swift will reenter the atmosphere at 5:19 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), plus or minus two hours. The earliest window for reentry opens around 3 a.m. Wednesday. NASA has not changed its estimates as of yet. This article was updated at 6 p.m. EST on Tuesday (Nov. 3). NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth as early as tonight (Nov. 3), the space agency says. According to NASA's latest estimates , shared yesterday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft will likely reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could plunge down as early as this evening. body: أسفرت عملية أمنية مشتركة بين مصالح الأمن الوطني والجمارك جرى تنفيذها زوال اليوم الثلاثاء بميناء طنجة المتوسط، عن إجهاض عملية للتهريب الدولي للمخدرات والمؤثرات العقلية وحجز ما مجموعه 971 كيلوغراما من مخدر الكوكايين. وقد تم حجز هذه الشحنات من مخدر الكوكايين خلال عمليات المراقبة الحدودية المشتركة بين مصالح الأمن والجمارك، حيث تم العثور على صفائح الكوكايين ضمن حاوية للتبريد كانت على متن باخرة تحمل علم دولة في أمريكا اللاتينية. وقد سمحت المعطيات الأولية للبحث بتحديد مسار الحاوية التي كانت تنقل هذه الشحنات من مخدر الكوكايين، والتي انطلقت من ميناء في دولة البرازيل وكانت متوجهة نحو أحد الموانئ في غرب إفريقيا. وقد تم فتح بحث قضائي في هذه النازلة من طرف المصلحة الولائية للشرطة القضائية بطنجة تحت إشراف النيابة العامة المختصة، للكشف عن جميع الظروف والملابسات المحيطة بهذه العملية الإجرامية، في حين تم تكليف المكتب المركزي الوطني (مكتب أنتربول الرباط) التابع للمديرية العامة للأمن الوطني بمباشرة عمليات التنسيق والتعاون الدولي للكشف عن الشبكة الإجرامية المتورطة في هذه العملية. المقالة إحباط تهريب 971 كيلوغرام كوكايين بميناء طنجة fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: قررت اللجنة العلمية للمؤشرات ببورصة البيضاء مراجعة قواعد تدبير مؤشر “MASI”، بهدف تكييفها مع التطورات التي يعرفها السوق، ومواكبة دخول مصدرين ومستثمرين جدد، إلى جانب الاستجابة لمطالب الفاعلين في السوق. وأفادت اللجنة، عقب اجتماعها المنعقد في 30 أكتوبر 2026، بأن التعديلات المرتقبة ستشمل شروط وكيفيات إدراج القيم الجديدة، ومنهجية احتساب الأسهم العائمة، فضلا عن طرق تحيين معاملاتها ومعاملات التسقيف، وكيفية التعامل مع الحالات الاستثنائية، والآجال المحددة لنشر مراجعات المؤشر قبل دخولها حيز التنفيذ. ومن المنتظر أن تستكمل هذه الأشغال، التي تتم في إطار لجنة المؤشرات، خلال شهر واحد، على أن يتم الإعلان عن القواعد الجديدة قبل الشروع في تطبيقها، بما يتيح لمختلف الفاعلين في المنظومة الاستعداد للتغييرات المرتقبة. وفي انتظار اعتماد القواعد المعدلة، قررت اللجنة، بصفة انتقالية، إعادة العمل بمعاملات الأسهم العائمة والتسقيف التي كانت معتمدة في احتساب أوزان مختلف القيم المدرجة ضمن مؤشر “MASI” قبل المراجعة السنوية المنجزة في 29 أكتوبر 2026، على أن يستمر هذا الإجراء إلى حين دخول قواعد التدبير الجديدة حيز التنفيذ. المقالة بورصة البيضاء تشرع في تحيين قواعد تدبير مؤشر “مازي” fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

body: يرتقب رفع السن الأقصى لاجتياز مباريات توظيف أطر التعليم إلى 40 سنة، بعدما أكد محمد نبيل بنعبد الله، وزير التربية الوطنية والتعليم الأولي والتكوين المهني والتأهيل، عزمه مراجعة السن المعتمد حاليا، وذلك خلال كلمة له أمام لجنة التعليم والثقافة والاتصال بمجلس النواب. ويأتي هذا التوجه في ظل استمرار المطالب بإلغاء شرط تسقيف سن الولوج إلى مهنة التعليم، الذي أثار جدلا واسعا منذ تحديده في 30 سنة، حيث اعتبره عدد من حاملي الشهادات الجامعية إجراء إقصائيا لا يراعي مبدأ تكافؤ الفرص، خاصة أن النظام الأساسي العام للوظيفة العمومية يحدد 45 سنة سقفا أقصى لولوج الوظائف العمومية. وكانت وزارة التربية الوطنية قد رفعت، في أكتوبر 2025، السن الأقصى لاجتياز مباريات التعليم من 30 إلى 35 سنة، غير أن القرار لم يضع حدا للاعتراضات المطالبة بإلغاء هذا الشرط بشكل نهائي. وسبق لبنعبد الله أن أعلن، يوم 21 أكتوبر الماضي، استعداده لمراجعة السن المعتمد والاستجابة للمطالب المطروحة. المقالة بنعبد الله يعلن رفع سن اجتياز مباريات التعليم إلى 40 سنة fمنشورة على جريدة الصباح .

title: Mars-bound astronauts could face years of heart scarring, rat study hints
summary: Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.
body: Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints. The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One , found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis , which is known to increase the risk of heart failure. This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation. But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats ( 80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth. title: Traces of ancient blood found in 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil, new study claims
summary: Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.
body: Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims. However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells. In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS , the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin. The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali . While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils , this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones. "Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. body: Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself. The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians , it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape. Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. title: Blue whales have gone missing off the Galápagos. Scientists think El Niño could be why.
summary: Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.
body: For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale. The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year. This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing. Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant. body: The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today. Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang , the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light. Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe." body: You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years. "It's all in the fine print," John Maisey , the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark." The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes , an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin. title: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
summary: Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?
body: Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors. In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models. RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development. This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input. body: Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome , according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age. Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as " Venus figurines " ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered. Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced , experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. title: Hepatitis B could surge, infecting millions more in childhood, under proposed CDC guidance
summary: A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.
body: A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts. Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice . The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series. title: Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders came from same 'ultravoyager' group
summary: Members of the same people who settled Easter Island also discovered Hawaii, a new study finds.
body: Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders genetically descend from the same "ultravoyager" Polynesian group that crossed vast distances of ocean to reach these remote islands, a new study finds. Easter Island (also known as Rapa Nui) and Hawaii are part of Polynesia, a group of more than 1,000 islands spread over an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly equal to the areas of North and South America combined. Hawaii and Easter Island are the farthest of these isles from each other, at about 4,500 miles (7,200 kilometers) apart — around the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru. The researchers discovered the connection by analyzing the genomes of 1,050 modern individuals across Polynesia, including 317 Native Hawaiians and 12 Easter Islanders. "Each person's genome contains genetic code from both parents, and from all four grandparents, and their parents, and so on," study co-author Alexander Ioannidis , a computational geneticist at Stanford University, told Live Science. The galaxy, which the researchers observed as it appeared just 2.1 billion years after the Big Bang, is the most distant ring galaxy ever found. The ring galaxy, known as GS18660, may be the result of a collision between two galaxies, the researchers reported in their study, published Sept. 8 in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics . title: Scientists invent implant that can transform sugar in the blood to treat type 2 diabetes
summary: An experimental medical device uses a tiny amount of electricity to spark a chemical reaction and remove extra sugar from the bloodstream.
body: An experimental medical implant that removes excess sugar from the blood has shown promise in treating diabetes and obesity in tests with lab mice. Coupled with a continuous glucose monitor, which tracks blood sugar levels in real time, the tiny device is designed to adjust blood sugar levels according to a patient's needs. It does so using a chemical reaction powered by electricity. In the mouse experiments, it prevented sudden insulin spikes and promoted fat loss. The implant, described Oct. 22 in the journal Science , could offer a completely new way to treat diabetes and obesity, study co-author Martin Fussenegger , a professor of biotechnology and bioengineering at ETH Zurich, told Live Science in an email. His team is now working toward testing the device in additional lab animals, and eventually, humans. About 790 million people have type 2 diabetes globally, and over 1 billion have obesity. People with obesity often have insulin resistance , in which cells don't respond to insulin well and can't take in the sugar they need from the blood. title: A psychologist explains his theory for why orcas are attacking boats
summary: Live Science spoke with comparative psychologist Christian Frings to discuss a new theory for why orcas are attacking yachts.
body: Over the past six years , orcas have made headlines for a unique behavior: Some individuals have repeatedly damaged or destroyed rudders on boats. The behavior has prompted a wide range of explanations, including that it's playful , a form of revenge , a warning against getting too close to the pod, or even a type of cultural transmission , in which one orca observes another interacting with a boat and then imitates it. But Christian Frings , a cognitive psychologist who studies how humans control their actions, thinks it could be deliberate. While Frings, who is also chair of general psychology and methodology at Trier University in Germany, does not study orcas directly, he believes that theories developed to explain human behavior could provide insight into this orca behavior. Orcas ( Orcinus orca ), he said, may be a "test case" for whether a wide variety of species can anticipate how their actions will change the environment and then take those actions deliberately, with the goal of making those changes. body: A pioneering NASA space telescope is no more. According to a NASA announcement , the Swift team shut down the telescope's science operations Tuesday (Oct. 20) after the observatory fell too low in its orbit to continue taking reliable measurements of the cosmos. In the coming weeks, Swift will drop even further, eventually passing a point of no return and taking a fiery plunge through Earth's atmosphere. The observatory is the latest victim of intense solar activity , which increases the drag on satellites in Earth orbit and makes it harder for spacecraft to stay aloft. Swift has been losing altitude for a while, but the final straw came in August, when a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed, ending with the would-be rescue craft burning up in the atmosphere after a series of hardware malfunctions. title: A neglected particle from the dawn of time could explain why everything in the universe exists
summary: A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.
body: A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang ‪—‬ changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all. The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. title: 'A potential glimpse into the future': Climate change has triggered 'permafrost landslides' with house-size blocks of ice in Canada
summary: For the first time, researchers have identified a new type of landslide of permafrost in Canada's Northwest Territories.
body: There's a new type of landslide affecting northern latitudes, and it could affect more areas as the planet continues to warm. These landslides, called permafrost detachment slides, occur in areas with relatively thin permafrost and seem to be a long-term impact of wildfire in these environments, according to a paper published Sept. 23 in the journal Geophysical Research Letters . Such slides have not been observed in the region before and may be unprecedented over the past 10,000 years or more, said study leader Joseph Young , who completed the work as part of his doctoral degree at the University of Alberta. "It has been stable, and then it just flipped a switch, essentially," Young told Live Science. Young and his colleagues were doing field observations in Canada's Northwest Territories when they noticed large landslide scars in valleys that have long hosted stable permafrost, which is sediment that remains frozen year-round. title: Colorectal cancer cases in kids have risen sixfold over past 2 decades ‪—‬ researchers are racing to understand why
summary: While rare, colorectal cancer is becoming more common in kids, teens and young adults, and the disease appears particularly aggressive in this age group.
body: More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease. While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society . Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S. Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50 . The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. They created agricultural lands in the region's desert landscape, and their archaeological record includes monumental temples, water canals, pottery, metallurgy, textiles and a distinctive form of art. In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold , cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time.
